standard.title: Language use at home and school
standard.description: explore how language is used differently at home and school depending on the relationships between people
standard.prior_knowledge: Students bring informal oral language from home, family and community contexts. They have not yet been asked to consciously observe and reflect on how language changes across different relationship contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can explain that language choices (words, tone, phrasing) change depending on the relationship between speakers, giving examples from both home and school contexts.

nodes.label: Language varies by context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that different situations call for different language — that how you speak changes depending on where you are.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of language that is used at school but not at home, or vice versa.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss examples of language used differently at school versus home, noting that the setting affects how we speak.
wider: Compare language used in multiple school settings — in the classroom, at lunch, on the playground — and discuss how it shifts across each
Compare language used in multiple home settings — with parents, siblings, grandparents — and identify what changes

response_modes.reason: Students at Foundation may initially treat 'school language' as a fixed thing — the misconception is that language is constant rather than contextually variable. More settings help break the exemplar convergence on a single school/home contrast.

success_criteria: Student can name at least one situation where they would speak differently (e.g. talking to a teacher vs talking to a friend).
Student can say why the language is different in those two situations.

nodes.label: Relationships shape language choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that the relationship between people — not just the setting — is what shapes language choices.
nodes.minimum_width: Give one example of how language changes depending on whether you are talking to a teacher or a friend.
nodes.typical_width: Identify how language changes across relationship types: teacher/student, parent/child, sibling/friend, shopkeeper/customer; recognise that formal vs informal language choices relate to relationship roles.
wider: Examine characters in picture books and identify language that shows the relationship between them
Explore how language in texts by First Nations Australian authors reflects relationship protocols and community roles
Investigate how language might differ when interacting with a known versus unknown adult

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of relationship types and associated language patterns — parent/child, teacher/student, peers, community members — before the generalisation becomes robust. A single contrast pair is insufficient.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of relationship types ACARA names is genuinely rich — parent/child, teacher/student, siblings, friends, shopkeepers — and each offers a distinct language register exploration. Advancing students can investigate how these vary within and across cultures.
success_criteria: Student can name at least two different relationships and explain how language would be different in each.
Student can give a specific example of a word or phrase that would or wouldn't be used in a particular relationship context.

nodes.label: Asking, expressing and requesting appropriately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use context-appropriate language when asking for things, expressing opinions or making requests, and can explain why they chose those words.
nodes.minimum_width: Use appropriate language to make one request or express one opinion in a school context.
nodes.typical_width: Ask relevant questions, express requests and share opinions in ways that suit the context; reflect on why the language chosen was appropriate for that context.
wider: Role-play the same request (e.g. asking for help) in three different contexts — with a teacher, a classmate, and a family member — and compare the language used
Explore how characters in stories ask for things and evaluate whether their language was appropriate for the relationship
Investigate how language used in requests differs across culturally diverse contexts represented in classroom texts

response_modes.reason: Students must bring together: knowing the relationship context, choosing appropriate register, and producing the language — three elements that now need to work together in performance. This is where the concept and the capability unite.

success_criteria: Student can make an appropriate request or express an opinion in a school context using suitable words and tone.
Student can explain why they chose the language they used for that context.
Student can identify at least one adjustment they would make to the same request in a different relationship context.
